q: Your team's velocity has dropped sharply over two sprints. What should you do FIRST?
options: Reassign the slowest members to other teams
Meet the team to understand the root cause of the slowdown
Escalate the performance issue to the sponsor
Add more people to the next sprint
explain: 'First' means assess before acting. Understand the root cause with the team — never remove people or escalate prematurely.

q: A requirement might be affected by a regulation that may change next year. How do you treat this?
options: Log it as an issue and resolve it now
Treat it as a risk and update the risk register
Stop the project immediately
Submit a change request
explain: 'Might/may' = a risk. It hasn't happened, so update the risk register & risk management plan rather than the issue log.

q: A team member tells you they feel unmotivated. What's the best response?
options: Offer a bonus to boost morale
Replace them to protect the schedule
Find out what personally motivates them and act on it
Tell them to focus on the deadline
explain: Servant leaders investigate the personal cause of demotivation and respond to it; they don't bribe, replace, or pressure.

q: A stakeholder asks you to add a feature mid-project. What do you do?
options: Add it quickly since it's small
Refuse — the scope is locked
Assess the impact, then run it through the formal change control process
Ask the sponsor to approve it directly
explain: Never implement changes yourself or refuse outright. Assess impact on all constraints, then go through integrated change control.

q: The customer says a finished deliverable doesn't meet their needs, but it passed QA testing. What process matters here?
options: Control Quality
Validate Scope
Define Scope
Control Procurements
explain: QA (Control Quality) checks correctness; the customer's acceptance is Validate Scope. Acceptance is the issue here.

q: In an agile project the Product Owner refuses to prioritize the backlog, calling everything valuable. You should…
options: Prioritize the backlog yourself
Train the PO on the benefits of prioritization
Escalate to the sponsor
Build all features at once
explain: Only the PO prioritizes. If they won't, coach/train them on the benefit — never take over the role.

q: A stakeholder asks for the exact project budget before planning is complete. What do you tell them?
options: Give the charter's range as the final number
Ask them to wait until planning is finished
Provide a definitive ±5% estimate now
Escalate the request to finance
explain: The charter offers only a range. A precise budget comes after planning, so ask them to wait.

q: During production you find scattered defects with no clear pattern. Which tool helps locate where errors concentrate?
options: Scatter diagram
Check-sheet
Decision tree
Tornado chart
explain: A check-sheet tabulates results to reveal error concentration so you can prioritize a response.

q: A control chart shows one data point far outside the limits. This is a…
options: Common cause — ignore it
Special cause — investigate it
Specification limit breach
Precision error
explain: A point requiring investigation is a special cause (a defect), unlike common-cause normal variation.

q: Two team members are in conflict over schedules. What's the preferred first approach?
options: Withdrawal until tempers cool
Forcing a decision as PM
Confrontation/problem-solving to address the source
Escalate to the functional manager
explain: Confrontation (problem-solving) is the most preferred technique; understand the source first. Escalation is a last resort.

q: You need more skilled hands but the PMO has no spare staff. Who do you approach?
options: The sponsor for new hires
The functional manager about availability
HR to recruit externally
The customer to extend the deadline
explain: Check the functional manager's availability before the PMO; the PM negotiates resources with the FM.

q: A remote, multicultural team keeps misunderstanding instructions on a complex task. Best communication choice?
options: A quick phone call
Informal chat messages
Formal written communication so all receive the same info
A single recorded video
explain: Complex problems plus cultural/remote differences call for extensive formal written communication.

q: A stakeholder complains they aren't getting useful status updates. What do you do?
options: Send more frequent reports immediately
Review the communications/engagement plan to learn what they need
Invite them to manage the project
Escalate to the sponsor
explain: Go back to the comms/stakeholder engagement plan and find out what they actually need before acting.

q: While planning responses for a known risk, the team identifies a brand-new risk. You should…
options: Stop and re-run Identify Risks immediately
Ignore it until monitoring
Document it as a secondary risk and keep planning
Escalate it to the sponsor
explain: Newly found risks during response planning are secondary risks — document them and continue planning.

q: An identified-but-unplanned risk has just been triggered. What's your response?
options: Qualify the risk
Implement a workaround
Add it to the watchlist
Run quantitative analysis
explain: A triggered, unplanned risk needs a workaround. Qualifying applies only when it hasn't triggered.

q: A vendor invoices for far more than the contract states. What's the appropriate action?
options: Stop all payments permanently
Terminate the contract
Issue a breach-of-contract notice, then discuss
Pay it to keep the relationship
explain: A T&C violation like over-invoicing warrants a breach notice, followed by discussion — not termination or stopping payment.

q: Seller selection will hinge on technical approach rather than price. Which document term applies?
options: Bid
Quotation
Tender
Proposal
explain: 'Proposal' is used when technical capability/approach is paramount; bid/tender/quotation are price-based.

q: A project is being terminated early. What must still happen?
options: Nothing — just release the team
Formally close it via Close Project or Phase
Skip lessons learned since it failed
Return the budget to finance only
explain: Even terminated projects are formally closed through Close Project or Phase, including lessons learned.

q: Who provides the final sign-off on project closure?
options: The project manager
The PMO
The sponsor
The functional manager
explain: The sponsor signs off on closure, after all work is verified, delivered, and accepted.

q: A question says a safety hazard has emerged that endangers workers right now. What do you do?
options: Assess the impact and review the plan first
Stop work immediately and start change control
Log it as a risk for later
Ask the sponsor for guidance
explain: Dire safety consequences are the exception to 'think first' — stop work and begin the change control process.

q: During a retrospective, two developers trade sharp remarks about code reviews. The team charter they drafted says reviews are finished within one working day, and neither has followed it. How should the project manager handle this?
options: Meet each developer one-on-one to reinforce the review commitment
Coach each developer privately on the one-day review commitment
Propose a review rotation that spreads the code review workload across the team
Facilitate a team discussion on honoring the review agreement they created
explain: The team wrote the charter, so the team should address breaches of it. A servant leader facilitates that conversation rather than enforcing it individually or imposing a new process.

q: An eyewear retailer's store-rollout teams use different checklists. Openings succeed, but quality varies by team. What should the project manager do?
options: Assign the best-performing team to handle all of the future store openings
Allow teams to continue using their own checklists
Consolidate best practices into one standard organizational checklist
Let each team keep its own checklist since openings succeed
explain: Variation shows an improvement opportunity. Standardizing best practices updates organizational assets.

q: A consumer electronics firm is moving to a product-centric operating model. The project's functional team members will join permanent product teams. What should the project manager do next?
options: Keep the current team structure until the project finishes
Let the product team leads decide on the members' reassignments later
Retain functional reporting lines through project completion
Plan the members' transition with the new product team leaders
explain: Organizational change affects project resources. Required actions must be determined with the new structure's leaders.

q: A grocery chain's loyalty app has shipped twelve releases. The sponsor asks whether it is delivering the promised increase in basket size. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Confirm that basket-size metrics are tracked against the benefit target
Show the sponsor the volume of releases completed to date
Report the number of features delivered across the twelve releases
Survey the app's users about their satisfaction with the recent releases
explain: The question is about benefits, not output. A measurement system tied to the benefit target answers it.

q: A localization team spans six countries. Quieter linguists rarely speak in planning sessions, and their later written comments often hold the best solutions. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Rotate the planning facilitator role among the leads in each of the regions
Ask quieter linguists to share their views verbally in sessions
Add asynchronous written input before planning discussions conclude
Encourage the quieter linguists to speak up more during planning
explain: The evidence shows written input works for these members. Supporting varied styles means adapting the process, not pushing people to change theirs.

q: A parcel locker rollout met every milestone, but municipal partners say they expected placement input that never happened. Placement criteria were in the signed plan. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Pause the remaining rollout until the municipalities approve every placement
Review the signed plan with the municipalities to show what was agreed
Engage the municipalities on remaining placements and acknowledge the gap
Examine the placement criteria in the plan with municipal partners
explain: Partner satisfaction matters even when the plan was followed. Reviewing the plan defends the past; engaging on what remains responds to their expectations.

q: A mattress factory's previous line installation suffered commissioning delays. The new line's project plan makes no reference to that project. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Use the previous project's lessons to adjust the commissioning plan
Add extra time to commissioning in case of similar delays
Ask the previous project's manager to join the new line's commissioning team
Include a commissioning schedule buffer just in case
explain: Lessons learned should shape planning. A generic buffer ignores the specific causes already known.

q: A date exporter's packaging project learns that a key importing country will ban certain plastics next year. What should the project manager do?
options: Finish the current packaging design, then adapt it for the ban
Complete the approved design and adjust it afterward
Wait for the regulation's final text before changing anything
Assess the ban's impact and reprioritize the packaging work
explain: A known regulatory change should reshape priorities now. Finishing first creates avoidable rework.

q: A food delivery team's retrospectives produce improvement ideas, but the improvement process itself has not changed in two years. What should the project manager do next?
options: Rotate the retrospective facilitator role among team members each sprint
Run more frequent retrospectives to generate more ideas
Inspect and adapt the improvement process itself with the team
Increase retrospective frequency to gather more ideas
explain: Continuous improvement processes also need updating. More of the same process yields more of the same results.

q: A salon franchise's new product line contains a dye ingredient that one export market restricts. Sales there are 15% of revenue. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Release everywhere and adjust the formula afterward
Launch in all markets and reformulate for that one later
Determine the compliance approach for that market before launch
Remove that export market from the product line's sales plan permanently
explain: Compliance needs must be addressed before entering the market. Launching first risks penalties.

q: A kiln upgrade's governance board asks for earned value data in its quarterly pack. The project currently reports milestone status alone. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Adapt the reporting to include the earned value data the board requires
Review whether milestone status already gives the board enough insight
Provide earned value figures to the board whenever significant variances arise
Assess if milestone reporting meets the board's needs as it stands
explain: The board stated its requirement, so the project should support the governance process. Questioning whether the request is needed is not the project's call.

q: A meat plant expansion will use a new refrigerant. The team has not classified which regulations apply to it. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Engage the refrigerant supplier to take care of the compliance requirements
Review the current refrigerant's rules for the new installation
Identify and classify the regulations that apply to the refrigerant
Examine existing refrigerant regulations for use in this case
explain: A new substance may fall under different rules. Compliance categories must be classified, not borrowed.

q: An EV charging network's installation schedule depends on a utility's grid connection approvals, which the project does not control. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Plan installations on the assumption of typical approval times
Schedule installations assuming approvals arrive on standard timelines
Coordinate with the utility and model approvals as external dependencies
Start installations now and connect each charger as soon as its approval arrives
explain: External dependencies must be coordinated and shown in the schedule. Assuming standard timelines hides a key risk.

q: A multi-site trial's sponsor requires monthly enrollment reports in a specific regulatory format. Site teams currently submit data in assorted spreadsheets. What should the project manager do?
options: Analyze site spreadsheets to see how fields match the required format
Define a standard site data template aligned to the sponsor's format
Ask the sponsor to accept the sites' existing spreadsheet formats
Review each site's spreadsheet to map its fields to the sponsor format
explain: The reporting requirement is known and fixed. Standardizing inputs at the source fixes it permanently; mapping each sheet repeats the effort every month.

q: A dredging project's register lists weather risks with owners assigned. One owner has left the company, and storm season starts next month. What should the project manager do next?
options: Reassess the weather risks' scores before the storm season
Assign the risk to a new owner and confirm the response is ready
Take personal ownership of the weather risks until a new owner is found
Review the weather risks to update their probability scores
explain: Every risk needs an active owner to execute responses. Rescoring does not fill that gap.

q: A yield-analytics team discovered a defect pattern a sister fab's team could use. Teams at the two fabs share tools but rarely talk. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Email the defect pattern findings to the sister fab's team
Upload the analysis to the shared tool so the other team can find it
Create a recurring forum where both fab teams share findings
Send the sister fab a written summary of the defect pattern
explain: The barrier is the lack of interaction, not access. Fostering an environment for ongoing exchange solves this case and future ones.

q: On a student portal project, a new team member openly dismisses ideas in stand-ups. The team's working agreement was set before this member joined. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Share the existing working agreement with the new member privately
Revisit the working agreement with the team, including the new member
Give the new member the agreement and discuss it one-on-one
Pair the new member with an experienced colleague for the next few sprints
explain: The new member never helped shape the ground rules. Co-creating them with the whole team builds the buy-in that a private briefing cannot.

q: A fish-farm sensor installation uses a vendor specialist who will leave after commissioning. Local staff will maintain the system. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Request the vendor's maintenance manual before the specialist leaves
Obtain the full system documentation from the vendor at handover
Pair local staff with the specialist during installation and commissioning
Add remote vendor support to the maintenance contract for after commissioning
explain: Those who will maintain the system must learn it while the expert is present. Manuals help, but working alongside the specialist transfers the know-how.

q: A crew-scheduling system has delivered all scope. Operations will accept handover once support staff are trained, which is not yet complete. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Complete the support training before the formal handover
Review the scope to confirm all deliverables are truly complete
Close the project and let operations arrange training
Assess the deliverables again to verify scope completion
explain: Scope is complete; transition readiness is not. Readiness, here training, must be validated before handover.

q: A furnace rebuild sponsor expects zero production loss, while plant engineering assumes a two-week stop. Neither assumption appears in the charter. What should the project manager do?
options: Examine the engineering basis for the two-week production stop
Surface both assumptions and agree on production impact before baselining
Plan the furnace rebuild schedule around the sponsor's zero-loss expectation
Review the engineering estimate to confirm a two-week stop is needed
explain: Two hidden, conflicting expectations exist. They must be made explicit and agreed before baselining; checking one side's estimate does not align anyone.

q: A reactor control upgrade relies on two engineers nearing retirement. Their knowledge is captured in procedures, but their troubleshooting judgment is not. What should the project manager do next?
options: Assess which troubleshooting steps are absent from the procedures
Record video walkthroughs of the current control procedures
Arrange shadowing so successors learn their troubleshooting judgment
Review the procedures to find where troubleshooting steps are missing
explain: Judgment is tacit knowledge that documents cannot hold. Shadowing transfers it; reviewing procedures only finds what is already known to be missing.

q: A new ride project has dozens of stakeholders, and the team treats every request with equal urgency. Planning meetings now overrun and decisions stall. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Limit planning meetings to stakeholders who attended the kickoff
Categorize stakeholders so engagement effort reflects influence and interest
Set a fixed agenda for planning meetings and timebox each stakeholder request
Restrict attendance to the original kickoff participants
explain: Equal treatment of every request signals that stakeholders were never categorized. Grouping by influence and interest focuses effort; trimming attendance is arbitrary.

q: A blood bank's donor app is funded quarterly. Finance asks how spending will be tracked when scope changes each sprint. What should the project manager propose?
options: Track spend per sprint against delivered value and the budget
Provide finance with quarterly totals at each period end
Report total spending to finance at the end of each quarter
Fix the scope for each quarter so the costs become fully predictable
explain: Spend tracking should span the life cycle. In agile, sprint-level burn against value gives finance timely insight; quarterly totals arrive too late.

q: Stakeholders of a booking platform complain they learn about feature changes only at release. The team maintains an information radiator in its own workspace. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Invite interested stakeholders to attend the team's daily stand-up
Notify stakeholders of feature changes when releases go live
Make the team's progress visible where stakeholders can access it
Send stakeholders a release announcement with each deployment
explain: The radiator exists but stakeholders cannot see it. Transparency means placing progress where they look; release notices still arrive too late.

q: A school renovation's change control board approved a classroom layout change. The contractor began work, but the drawings and schedule were not updated. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Review the change approval to confirm the contractor may proceed
Update the drawings and schedule to reflect the approved change
Ask the change board to re-approve the layout change
Examine the board decision to verify the change was approved
explain: The approval is not in doubt. Approved changes must be reflected in project documentation.

q: A battery cell project's resource histogram shows chemists overallocated in weeks 8 to 10, and the critical path does not run through their tasks. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Review the histogram with the chemists to confirm the overallocation
Use float on the chemists' tasks to smooth the overallocation
Bring additional chemists in for weeks 8 through 10
Analyze the weeks 8 to 10 workload to verify the peak is real
explain: The histogram already shows the problem, and the tasks have float. Resource smoothing within float resolves it at no cost.

q: A lab-informatics team learns that a quality lead, never consulted, can block release under internal rules. The team is four sprints in. What should the project manager do?
options: Add the quality lead to the register as a high-power stakeholder
Include the quality lead in the release-stage sign-off meeting
Engage the quality lead now to understand release expectations
Invite the quality lead to the final review before release
explain: A stakeholder who can block release must be engaged early. Late involvement invites rework, and a register entry alone is not engagement.

q: A drilling engineer and the logistics planner disagree on rig mobilization order. Both positions are technically sound, and the mobilization window closes in two days. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Hold the decision until updated weather data favors one order
Facilitate in-depth problem solving until both of their goals are fully met
Work with both to find an order that fully meets each one's goals
Help them reach a middle-ground order each can accept within the window
explain: Collaboration takes time the window does not allow. With two sound positions and a hard deadline, a compromise is the practical resolution.

q: After a mine automation pilot, the same misunderstanding of the end state keeps resurfacing in each new work package. Earlier clarifications were sent by email and acknowledged. What should the project manager do next?
options: Send a consolidated clarification of the end state to all package leads
Find out why the end state is still misread despite earlier clarifications
Add a clear end state description to every new work package's kickoff deck now
Issue one combined note restating the end state to every package lead
explain: Clarifications were acknowledged yet the problem recurs, so more messages will not help. The pattern calls for identifying the root cause of the misunderstanding.

q: A facility firm's building system upgrade faces a supplier issue that affects three stakeholders' areas. Each has proposed a different fix. What should the project manager do next?
options: Bring the affected stakeholders together to agree on one approach
Implement the solution from the most impacted stakeholder
Ask the supplier to choose the fix it prefers, since it caused the issue
Select the fix proposed by the stakeholder most affected
explain: Issues affecting several stakeholders should be resolved collaboratively. Picking one proposal leaves the others unaligned.

q: A recycling plant project sees an opportunity: a new sorting technology could halve processing time if adopted in the next phase. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Note the opportunity for consideration in a future project
Accept the opportunity passively and take advantage of it if it arises
Plan an opportunity response to capture the technology's benefit
Record it in lessons learned for future projects
explain: Positive risks deserve active responses such as exploit or enhance. Passive acceptance leaves the benefit to chance.

q: A payments team's sprint reviews are well attended, yet stakeholders raise concerns weeks later by email. Reviews consist of demos with no discussion time. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Build structured feedback time into each sprint review
Lengthen the demos so stakeholders see features in depth
Extend the demos to show more detail on each feature
Send a follow-up survey after each sprint review
explain: The missing piece is a feedback loop inside the review. A survey keeps feedback delayed; longer demos add more one-way content.

q: A consulting team will hand a cost-reduction model to the client's analysts. The analysts have attended every demo but have never run the model themselves. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Provide the analysts with recordings of every demo for reference
Deliver a detailed user manual and a quick reference guide with the model
Share the demo recordings so analysts can revisit them later
Have the analysts run the model with the team's support before handover
explain: Watching is not doing. Hands-on practice with support ensures the knowledge actually transfers.

q: A coworking operator is negotiating with an app vendor. The vendor proposes a large upfront fee, while the operator wants to test market fit within six months. Which negotiation strategy is best?
options: Seek milestone payments tied to market validation results
Accept the fee in exchange for longer support coverage
Negotiate a discount on the upfront fee for the full contract
Seek a lower upfront fee while keeping the full commitment
explain: The operator's goal is to learn before committing. Payments tied to validation align the deal to that goal; discounts keep the full exposure.

q: Field crews on a rural fiber rollout keep asking why the network design favors coverage over speed. The design rationale was approved by the steering board and appears on the project site. How should the project manager respond?
options: Explain the coverage rationale in crew huddles using examples from the field
Point the crews to the approved design rationale on the project site
Direct the crews to the steering board's published design rationale
Invite crew representatives to attend the next steering board design review session
explain: The rationale is already published, so pointing to it again will not build understanding. Promoting the shared vision in the crews' own context is what closes the gap.

q: A theater's ticketing modernization team lacks UX skills. A marketing designer could join part-time, or a contractor could join full-time. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Use the marketing designer part-time to keep costs low
Have the developers handle the UX tasks using standard design templates
Bring in the full-time contractor as a dedicated team member
Engage the part-time marketing designer for the UX tasks
explain: Agile teams work best with dedicated, cross-functional members. Part-time members create context switching and waiting.

q: A post-production team keeps missing internal handoffs. Editors say colorists change specs midstream; colorists say editors never confirm receipt. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Hold a weekly joint review where both groups go over each of the missed handoffs
Have the editors acknowledge each colorist spec in writing
Ask editors to confirm receipt of every spec sent by the colorists
Define handoff responsibilities and confirmation points with both groups
explain: Both complaints point to an undefined handoff. Fixing only one side moves the gap, and a weekly review discusses it without solving it.

q: A laundry service's routing app team holds retrospectives, but action items are rarely implemented. The same issues reappear each sprint. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep a complete list of actions from each retrospective
Hold retrospectives less often so each action gets more of the team's attention
Commit to a few improvements and add them to the next sprint backlog
Record all retrospective actions in a shared improvement log
explain: Continuous improvement needs implementation. Putting a few actions into the backlog makes them real work; logs do not.

q: A stadium app's teams use data from ticketing, concessions, and security. Leaders want a decision on next quarter's features, but no one has compared usage across sources. What should the project manager do next?
options: Let the leadership group decide features based on experience
Prioritize features by the leaders' collective judgment this time
Survey fans on which features they want next quarter
Consolidate the usage data to inform the feature decision
explain: Relevant data exists but has not been analyzed together. Collecting and analyzing it supports an informed decision.

q: A health insurer's claims project needs a decision that exceeds the project manager's spending authority. The governance framework has no threshold for this case. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Review past decisions to estimate a reasonable spending limit
Work with the sponsor to define the decision threshold and path
Analyze earlier approvals to infer a likely authority limit
Defer the decision until the next quarterly governance review meeting
explain: Governance escalation paths and thresholds should be defined, not inferred. Working with the sponsor establishes legitimate authority.

q: A commercial printer's workflow project has five open impediments. The team spreads its effort across all of them, and none gets resolved. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Log all five impediments for discussion at the next team retrospective
Prioritize impediments by impact and address the highest first
Assign one team member to each of the open impediments
Distribute the impediments evenly across team members
explain: Spreading effort thin resolves nothing. Impediments must be prioritized and highlighted by impact.

q: A museum's digital exhibit involves curators, educators, and donors. Early interviews show each group assumes the exhibit is mainly for them. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Design separate exhibit sections, each one tailored to a group's priorities
Share the interview findings with each group's lead by email
Run a workshop to agree on the exhibit's primary and secondary audiences
Create distinct exhibit zones reflecting each group's needs
explain: Expectations are identified but conflicting. A facilitated workshop aligns them; splitting the exhibit avoids the decision.

q: A paper mill automation project's deliverables have passed quality control. The plant owner has not yet formally accepted them. What should the project manager do next?
options: Hold an acceptance review of the deliverables with the plant owner
Mark the deliverables complete since they have passed the quality checks
Review the quality control results to confirm the work is complete
Examine the quality records to verify all deliverables passed
explain: Quality control confirms correctness; validating scope requires the customer's formal acceptance. Rechecking quality records does not obtain it.

q: An agritech firm needs a field sensor solution. Off-the-shelf sensors meet 80% of needs; custom development would take a year. Which delivery solution is most appropriate?
options: Develop custom sensors that meet every need from the start
Hold the decision until newer sensors appear
Buy off-the-shelf sensors and close the gap incrementally
Build a bespoke sensor solution covering all requirements
explain: Buying delivers most of the value now, and the remaining gap can be closed later. A year-long build delays all value.

q: A freight company's fleet tracking phase one is complete. Phase two starts next month with the same sponsor. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Review phase one's lessons before deciding on phase two
Roll phase one directly into phase two with the same sponsor
Obtain formal phase acceptance before mobilizing phase two
Assess phase one's lessons to inform the phase two decision
explain: Each phase closes formally with acceptance. A shared sponsor does not remove that step, and lessons inform the next phase only after closure.

q: A bridge rehabilitation scope statement is approved. While building the WBS, the team finds deck drainage is in the contract but in no work package. What should the project manager do?
options: Submit a change request so the drainage work can enter the scope
Review the WBS history to see why drainage was omitted
Assess whether drainage was left out of the WBS on purpose
Add the drainage work to the WBS as part of the agreed scope
explain: Drainage is already in the contract, so it is in scope. The WBS must capture all agreed work; no change request is needed and investigating the omission adds nothing.

q: A textile mill's quality plan targets fabric defects only. Customers now ask for water-use certification, which a sustainability initiative is pursuing. What should the project manager do next?
options: Track water usage outside the quality management plan
Report water-use figures separately from the quality plan
Add water-use criteria to the quality requirements and controls
Certify the mill's water use after the sustainability initiative is complete
explain: Customer-required sustainability criteria are quality requirements. Managing them inside quality controls ensures they are met and evidenced.

q: A dairy's milking automation project has an SPI of 0.95 and a CPI of 1.10 at midpoint. The sponsor asks for the expected total cost. What should the project manager provide?
options: The budget at completion as the expected total cost
An estimate at completion based on current cost performance
The original budget as the forecast for the final cost
A total cost projection derived from the schedule performance index
explain: Total cost forecasts come from the EAC, using CPI. The BAC is the plan, not the forecast, and SPI measures schedule, not cost.

q: A radar integration team receives conflicting direction from two functional managers in a weak matrix. Members ask the project manager which instruction to follow. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Work with both functional managers to agree on a single direction
Ask members to follow the direction of their own functional manager
Analyze which instruction better supports the baseline plan
Review both instructions against the approved project plan
explain: In a weak matrix the project manager lacks authority to overrule functional managers. Analysis against the plan cannot settle it; agreement between the managers can.

q: A port's container-tracking project lists efficiency as its value. Terminal operators, shipping lines, and customs each define efficiency differently. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Use the terminal operator's definition since it funds the project
Track one broad efficiency index that blends all three groups' definitions
Adopt the funding party's view of efficiency for the project
Define the specific value components with each key stakeholder group
explain: Value must be defined with key stakeholders. One party's view or a blended index hides what each group actually needs.

q: Two subcontractors on a housing project argue over sequencing in a site meeting. The disagreement surfaced right after the superintendent informally changed the pour schedule. What should the project manager do first?
options: Refer the sequencing dispute to the resolution clause defined in the subcontracts
Trace the dispute back to the pour schedule change with both subcontractors
Ask the subcontractors to propose a sequence they can both accept
Have both subcontractors negotiate a mutually acceptable sequence
explain: The conflict appeared after an undocumented change, which is the likely source. Identifying the source comes before negotiating sequences or invoking contract clauses.

q: A hotel's guest app shows high feature completion, but guest ratings for the app have dipped over two releases. Sprint reviews include internal staff only. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Bring guest feedback into sprint reviews alongside staff input
Shorten the release cadence to address rating issues sooner
Ask internal staff to represent guest views more strongly in reviews
Have front-desk staff speak for guests during sprint reviews
explain: External customers are missing from the feedback loop. Their expectations must be heard directly; staff proxies have not prevented the decline.

q: A desalination plant's procurement, quality, and risk plans were each approved separately. Integration now shows the procurement timeline clashes with quality hold points. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Review the procurement timeline to locate the conflicting hold points
Resolve the clash within one integrated plan before baselining
Examine the quality hold points to find where they clash with procurement
Log the timeline clash as a risk in the risk register
explain: The conflict is already found. Integrated planning means resolving dependencies across subsidiary plans before the baseline; re-examining either plan alone repeats the discovery.

q: A solar farm's monitoring software could go live per inverter group as each is installed, or all at once at commissioning. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Evaluate the cost of each go-live option before choosing the deployment approach
Release monitoring per inverter group as installations are completed
Assess both deployment options by cost to pick the cheaper one
Deploy monitoring for the whole farm once commissioning is complete
explain: Incremental release delivers value early and finds issues sooner. A cost-only comparison misses the value of early monitoring.

q: A call center's IVR redesign follows agile, but the client contract requires formal approval for scope changes above 10% of effort. What should the project manager do?
options: Manage backlog changes normally and seek formal approval above it
Submit every backlog change for formal client approval
Avoid making any backlog changes that could exceed the contract threshold
Route all backlog changes through formal approval
explain: Change control can be tailored: routine backlog changes flow normally, and those above the contract threshold get formal approval.

q: A studio upgrade sends a weekly 20-page report to all stakeholders. The sponsor admits she reads only the first page, while engineers say it lacks detail. What should the project manager do next?
options: Shorten the weekly report to a two-page summary for everyone
Add an executive summary at the front
Condense the report into a brief summary for all recipients
Tailor report content and depth to each audience's needs
explain: Different audiences need different depth. One report cannot serve both, so reports must be aligned to each stakeholder group's expectations.

q: A claims-automation team asks the project manager to attend steering meetings on their behalf because executives keep adding unplanned requests mid-sprint. How should the project manager respond?
options: Represent the team's capacity limits and route new requests to the backlog
Accept urgent executive requests and help the team fit them in
Ask executives to submit any future requests in writing directly to the team
Absorb the executives' requests and rebalance the current sprint
explain: The team asked to be represented. Acting as its voice and protecting the sprint by routing work through the backlog is the servant-leader response.

q: A launch vehicle engineer implemented a design improvement that cost nothing and passed tests. It was never submitted to change control. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Assess the test data to verify the improvement's safety
Review the test results to confirm the improvement is safe
Remove the improvement and restore the baseline design
Submit the improvement for review through change control
explain: Unapproved changes must go through change control. Test results do not replace configuration review.

q: During backlog refinement for a driver app, regional managers ask for features that contradict each other. None of them has seen the others' requests. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Make all regional requests visible and discuss trade-offs together
Have the product owner order the requests by expected value
Collect each region's rationale for its requests through individual interviews
Ask the product owner to rank the requests by business value
explain: No one sees the conflicts, so expectations cannot align. Transparency and joint discussion align them; ranking alone leaves each manager surprised later.

q: A penetration-testing team is new to working together and unsure how the engagement will run. Members are highly certified but have not agreed on how decisions are made. Which leadership approach is most appropriate now?
options: Let the experts self-organize, given their strong certifications
Give the team full latitude since every member is highly certified
Set clear expectations and structure while the team establishes norms
Coach members individually on their testing techniques before the kickoff
explain: Individual expertise does not make a team. In the forming stage, direction and clear expectations help the group establish how it works.

q: Signaling and civil teams on a rail upgrade dispute who owns trackside cabling. The responsibility assignment matrix shows both teams as responsible for that work package. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Update the matrix so that one team is accountable for the cabling package
Assess the overlap in cabling scope between the two teams' packages
Assign the cabling package to one combined signaling and civil crew instead
Review the cabling scope with both leads to see where it overlaps
explain: The source is already visible: the matrix lacks a single accountable owner. Reviewing or assessing the overlap restates what is known; the fix is clarifying accountability.

q: A ship refit's hotel and marine departments expect different handover dates. Each date is defensible, and both directors report to the same vice president. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Evaluate both handover dates against the schedule to find the impact
Facilitate a joint session where both directors agree on one date
Assess the schedule impact of each date before meeting the directors
Plan two staged handovers matching each department's date
explain: Both dates are already defensible, so more analysis adds little. The directors' expectations must be aligned in a facilitated discussion.

q: A vessel owner's representative has started making informal remarks about finish quality during yard visits. No formal complaint has been filed. What should the project manager do?
options: Review the remarks for a pattern before deciding how to respond
Increase the number of quality inspections on the current finishing work
Meet the representative to understand the concerns behind the remarks
Analyze the remarks to see whether a recurring theme emerges
explain: Informal remarks are an early satisfaction signal from the customer. Responding directly beats waiting for a pattern or reacting with more inspections.

q: A carpet manufacturer's e-commerce project assumed stable demand. A competitor just launched a cheaper machine-made line in the same market. What should the project manager do next?
options: Cut prices on the e-commerce site to match the competitor's new line
Reassess project priorities in light of the competitor's launch
Proceed with the approved scope as planned
Continue the project since the scope has been approved
explain: Market shifts can change what delivers value. The project should reassess its scope and backlog accordingly.

q: An automation team waits days for test hardware approvals from a central IT group. The team has raised this in stand-ups for three sprints. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Ask the team to plan their sprint work around the recurring approval delays
Work with central IT to remove the approval delay for the team
Note the delay in the impediment log for further tracking
Keep recording the delay as an impediment at each stand-up
explain: A recurring impediment needs action, not more tracking. Removing blockers outside the team's control is the servant leader's job.

q: A recruitment agency's candidate portal has a long backlog. Recruiters' feedback after each demo has shifted what they consider most useful. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Keep the initial backlog order to maintain team stability
Collect more recruiter feedback before making any changes to priorities
Complete the backlog in its original order to avoid churn
Reprioritize the backlog using recruiters' latest feedback and value
explain: Prioritizing by value and stakeholder feedback is the purpose of each demo. Ignoring it delivers less value.

q: A coatings plant's quality costs are rising due to rework of off-spec batches. Inspection is thorough, but defects are found late. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Increase inspection frequency to catch batches sooner
Rework off-spec batches in a dedicated line to save time
Inspect batches more often to detect defects earlier
Invest in prevention to stop off-spec batches earlier
explain: Prevention costs less than appraisal and failure. More inspection still pays for defects that should never occur.

q: A route-optimization project needs drivers' cooperation. Drivers recently rejected a similar tool because their shift input was collected and never acted on. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Collect drivers' shift input through a broader survey this time
Pilot the tool first with a group of volunteer drivers who are supportive
Show drivers how their input shapes the tool before asking for more
Run a larger survey to gather input from more of the drivers
explain: Trust was lost because input went nowhere. Visibly acting on input rebuilds trust; collecting more repeats the original mistake.

q: A portfolio analytics team's burnup chart shows scope rising as fast as completed work. Stakeholders believe the team is slowing down. What should the project manager do?
options: Push the team to deliver faster than scope is being added
Show stakeholders that scope growth is what delays completion
Ask the team to raise velocity to outpace the scope growth
Switch to a burndown chart so that progress looks clearer to stakeholders
explain: The burnup shows steady delivery with growing scope. Communicating the real cause is correct; pressuring the team misreads the data.

q: During a smelter upgrade, a vendor delivers equipment on time, but site tests show it misses one performance parameter in the contract. What should the project manager do next?
options: Review the test results again to confirm the parameter is missed
Modify the plant process to accommodate lower performance
Address the shortfall with the vendor under the contract terms
Examine the test data to verify the performance shortfall
explain: The tests already show the miss. Verifying that agreement objectives are met means acting under the contract, not retesting.

q: A golf course redevelopment estimate includes contingency for identified risks. The board also wants protection against unforeseen events. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Set a management reserve in addition to the contingency reserve
Analyze the register to find risks not yet listed
Review the risk register for events that are still unidentified
Increase the contingency reserve so it also covers unknown events
explain: Unforeseen events are unknown-unknowns, covered by management reserve. Contingency covers identified risks only, and reviewing the register cannot list the unknowable.

q: A police radio upgrade's project manager knows the organization requires ethics review for vendor gifts. A vendor has just offered tickets to the team. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Handle the offer as the organization's ethics policy requires
Evaluate if the gift's value could compromise objectivity
Assess whether the tickets' value could create a conflict
Ask the vendor to donate the tickets to a local charity on the team's behalf
explain: The organization's policy already governs gifts. Personal judgment of value bypasses the defined procedure.

q: A dealership group's CRM rollout has a fixed go-live and an agile configuration team. Executives want a schedule view they recognize. What should the project manager provide?
options: A full activity-level Gantt built from the team's backlog
Milestones for go-live with iteration plans beneath them
A detailed Gantt chart converted from the agile work
The team's burndown charts shared with executives
explain: A hybrid schedule fits a hybrid approach: milestones executives recognize, with iterations beneath. Converting the backlog into Gantt detail adds false precision.

q: A satellite payload customer and the integrator signed off the same requirements, yet in a design review each expected a different test campaign. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Submit a change request defining the integrator's test campaign
Review the signed requirements to determine which test scope is implied
Analyze the requirements document to settle the intended test scope
Facilitate a discussion to align both parties on the test campaign
explain: Both parties signed the same document and still disagree, so the text cannot settle it. Expectations must be aligned through facilitated discussion.

q: A public library's e-services portal must meet accessibility standards. The team plans to test accessibility just before final release. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Include accessibility checks in each iteration's definition of done
Train the developers on accessibility standards after the portal is released
Schedule a full accessibility audit at the end
Hire an accessibility auditor to test before final release
explain: Compliance should be measured continuously. Testing at the end finds issues when fixes cost most.

q: A footwear brand's product line project has a risk register last updated at kickoff. Several risks have since occurred or expired. What should the project manager do?
options: Archive the kickoff register and start a new register
Set a regular cadence to review and update the risk register
Replace the original register with a fresh version
Move the occurred risks into the issue log so they can be tracked
explain: Artifacts must be kept current through regular updates. A one-time refresh will go stale again.

q: A designer and a sourcing manager on a capsule collection keep clashing. You learn the designer's bonus rewards originality while the sourcing manager's rewards low unit cost. What should the project manager do next?
options: Set clear decision rights between design and sourcing for the whole collection
Facilitate a trade-off workshop for the designer and sourcing manager
Mediate a session where both agree on design and cost trade-offs
Work with their functional managers to align objectives behind the collection
explain: The context, opposing incentives, drives the conflict. Mediation treats the symptom and the clash will recur unless the objectives themselves are aligned.

q: A refinery turnaround needs scaffolding crews, cranes, and inspectors. The team estimated labor but not equipment or materials. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Refine the labor estimates with more detailed productivity rates
Estimate equipment and material needs alongside the labor estimates
Improve labor estimate accuracy using detailed crew productivity
Request the equipment from the contractors as the needs arise on site
explain: Resource planning covers physical as well as human resources. Refining labor further leaves the real gap open.

q: A menu-digitization team excels technically, but morale dropped after a key member left. Velocity is steady, yet members have stopped proposing ideas in reviews. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Meet the team to understand what changed and what support they need
Celebrate the team's consistent delivery at the next review
Recognize the team's steady velocity publicly to lift morale
Introduce an innovation sprint to restart idea generation in the team
explain: Steady velocity hides an engagement drop. Understanding the cause comes before choosing recognition or new formats.

q: An elder care provider is adopting agile for its resident app. Managers still expect detailed upfront plans and weekly signed reports. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Produce the detailed plans and signed reports managers expect
Provide managers with full upfront plans and weekly reports
Coach managers on agile practices while tailoring reports to them
Switch the project to a predictive approach to fit the managers' expectations
explain: Cultural transition needs coaching and some tailoring. Fully conforming to old habits blocks the change.

q: A fragrance company's e-commerce team estimates in hours, and estimates are consistently off. Stories vary widely in uncertainty. What should the project manager suggest?
options: Add a buffer to each hour estimate to absorb uncertainty
Have the lead developer estimate all stories for consistency
Shift to relative sizing such as story points for estimates
Pad hour-based estimates to account for unknowns
explain: Relative sizing handles uncertainty better than absolute hours. Padding hides the problem, and one estimator removes team insight.

q: An olive oil producer's traceability team is blocked by a labeling machine that fails intermittently. Engineers have tried three fixes. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Have the engineers attempt another repair on the labeler
Evaluate the blocker's impact and agree on an intervention strategy
Ask engineers to try a fourth fix on the labeling machine
Pause all traceability work until the labeling machine is fully reliable
explain: Repeated fixes have failed, so a strategy is needed. Understanding impact guides whether to work around, replace, or reprioritize.

q: A customs modernization project reports to three oversight bodies, each asking for different formats and frequencies. What should the project manager do?
options: Prepare a distinct report for each oversight body
Send all three oversight bodies the same consolidated weekly report
Agree on a governance structure defining reporting for all three
Produce separate reports in each body's requested format
explain: Reporting is part of governance and should be established deliberately. Ad hoc reports for each body multiply effort.

q: A tax agency must select a vendor for a filing portal. Two bids are close on price, and one vendor has a weak record on similar public projects. What should the project manager do next?
options: Apply the published selection criteria, including past performance
Ask both vendors to rebid with revised pricing and updated references
Choose the cheaper vendor because both meet requirements
Select the lower bid since the prices are close and both qualify
explain: Source selection must follow the published criteria, which typically weigh past performance. Price alone is not the rule.

q: A tractor maker's project uses a component from a country now facing new sanctions. Deliveries have not yet been affected. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Continue with the supplier since deliveries remain unaffected
Keep the current supplier as long as deliveries arrive
Assess the sanctions' impact on supply and plan alternatives
Stockpile the component for the rest of the project
explain: Geopolitical changes require proactive assessment. Waiting until deliveries stop removes options.

q: Midway through a tea estate's traceability project, the export market in the business case closed. The plan is on schedule and within budget. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Update the risk register to reflect the closure of the export market
Continue execution because the plan is on schedule and budget
Proceed as planned since performance is within the baseline
Revalidate the business value with the sponsor before continuing
explain: Good performance against a plan does not mean the plan is still worth doing. The project's continued business value must be confirmed.

q: A health ministry's records digitization depends on staff adopting new workflows. The ministry's culture strongly favors paper approvals. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Provide training on the new system's features to all staff before go-live
Launch the system and mandate its use for all approvals
Plan change activities addressing the preference for paper approvals
Go live and make the digital workflow mandatory for staff
explain: The organizational culture must be addressed for adoption. Mandates breed workarounds, and feature training ignores the cultural barrier.

q: A data center migration team rotates on-call duty. Each rotation rediscovers the same workarounds because solutions live in individual chat messages. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Hold a handover call between on-call shifts at each rotation
Set up a shared, searchable record of workarounds the team maintains
Pin the most useful workaround threads at the top of the team channel
Ask outgoing on-call members to brief incoming ones each rotation
explain: Knowledge is gathered but scattered. A maintained, searchable record makes it accessible to every rotation; verbal handovers repeat the loss.

q: An events platform team released a seating tool that works as specified. Early users rate it low, describing it as technically fine but not what they pictured. What should the project manager do?
options: Validate upcoming increments with users through early prototypes
Clarify the specification with users before the next release
Add an in-tool feedback form to collect user input on future releases
Have users review the written specs ahead of the next increment
explain: The spec was met, but expectations were not. Early prototypes expose mismatches; written specs already failed to do so.

q: A warehouse automation change was approved and implemented. Pickers say the new layout slows them, and they were never told about the change. What should the project manager do next?
options: Revert the layout to its previous configuration
Communicate the change and its rationale to pickers and seek feedback
Restore the old layout until the pickers adjust
Submit a new change request to adjust the layout based on picker complaints
explain: Implementing a change includes communicating it. Reverting before pickers understand it discards an approved decision.

q: A digital asset exchange's onboarding feature is nearly done. A new anti-money-laundering rule takes effect in three months. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Release the feature now and address the rule in a later version
Ask legal counsel to approve the onboarding feature as it is currently built
Ship the current feature and update it when the rule applies
Confirm the rule's requirements and prioritize them in the backlog
explain: Compliance requirements must be confirmed and planned. Releasing first creates rework against a known deadline.

q: A language school's course platform has a vague goal of better learner engagement. The team cannot agree on acceptance criteria. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Define measurable engagement outcomes with stakeholders to guide criteria
Begin building the first features and refine the criteria during sprint reviews
Have the team draft criteria from common industry practice
Let developers propose acceptance criteria based on best practice
explain: Scope cannot be defined against a vague goal. Measurable outcomes agreed with stakeholders give the team a basis for criteria.

q: An offshore wind project is 60% complete. Updated market forecasts cut expected electricity prices, but the project remains within budget. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Proceed with the plan because spending is on track
Continue as planned since cost performance is within budget
Reassess the business case using the updated price forecasts
Reduce the remaining scope to lower costs in line with the new prices
explain: Business value must be examined throughout the project. Budget performance says nothing about whether the expected returns still hold.

q: A toy company's holiday line must launch on a fixed date. The toys are well defined, but the companion app's features depend on testing with children. Which execution strategy is most appropriate?
options: Freeze all app features early to protect the launch date
Move the companion app's launch to a date after the holiday season ends
Fix the app scope now so that the launch date can be guaranteed
Fix the launch date and deliver app features in prioritized increments
explain: The date is fixed and app scope is uncertain, so scope should flex. Prioritized increments protect the date while learning from testing.

q: A pest control company's fleet project identified a fuel price risk. The response was implemented, and the sponsor asks for its current status. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Report the response's effectiveness and any residual risk
Inform the sponsor the risk is resolved since the response ran
Tell the sponsor the risk closed when the response was run
Share the original risk analysis with the sponsor
explain: A response does not close a risk by itself. The status of its impact, including residual risk, should be communicated.

q: A device project shows a CPI of 0.92 and an SPI of 1.05. The team is ahead of schedule, and the sponsor is pleased. What should the project manager do?
options: Continue as planned given the favorable schedule performance
Maintain the current pace since the project is ahead of schedule
Analyze the causes of the cost variance and report through governance
Slow the pace of work to bring schedule and cost performance into balance
explain: A CPI below 1 means overspending, which governance must see. Schedule gains do not offset cost overruns.

q: A creative director and the client's brand manager have a tense exchange over campaign tone. How client disputes are to be resolved was agreed in the engagement plan. What should the project manager do next?
options: Ask the creative director to prepare alternative tone concepts for the client
Assess the dispute to choose the best-fitting resolution technique
Evaluate which resolution style suits this tone dispute the best
Apply the dispute approach both parties agreed to in the engagement plan
explain: An agreed-on resolution strategy already exists, so the step is to implement it. Evaluating new styles reopens a decision the parties already made.

q: A sugar refinery's expansion is based on export quotas. A trade agreement under negotiation could change those quotas next year. What should the project manager do next?
options: Continue as planned since the agreement is not finalized
Monitor the negotiation and assess its impact on scope and benefits
Proceed with the plan until the agreement is signed
Reduce the expansion scope now in anticipation of lower export quotas
explain: External changes must be surveyed and their impact assessed early. Cutting scope on speculation is premature.

q: A tour operator's booking system relies on an old payment gateway with known security weaknesses. A breach would expose customer data. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Plan a response to reduce the gateway's security risk now
Transfer the risk by purchasing cyber insurance
Accept the risk since no breach has occurred so far
Retain the risk because the gateway has not been breached to date
explain: Known security weaknesses need a response that reduces exposure. Insurance compensates but does not protect customer data.

q: A confectionery plant's estimate was prepared from analogous data. The project is now in detailed design, and the sponsor asks for a budget baseline. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Use parametric estimates based on last year's costs at the confectionery plant
Develop bottom-up estimates from the design to set the baseline
Review the analogous estimate to check whether it still holds
Assess the analogous figures for continued accuracy
explain: Detailed design enables bottom-up estimating, the most accurate basis for a cost baseline. Rechecking the rough estimate keeps a weaker basis.

q: A wellness app's defects are found mostly in production. The team's definition of done includes code review but not automated tests. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Update the definition of done to include automated testing
Introduce a separate QA stage prior to every release
Assign a tester to review each story after the sprint
Add a dedicated testing phase before each production release
explain: Quality is built in through the definition of done. A late test phase adds delay and still finds defects late.

q: A set-top box deployment shows 80% of units installed, but call-center data reveals a spike in customer issues among installed homes. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Accelerate remaining installations to finish on schedule
Analyze installation records to validate the 80% progress figure
Include customer issue rates when assessing deployment progress
Review the installation count to confirm the 80% figure is right
explain: The count is not in doubt; what it measures is incomplete. Progress must include whether installs actually work.

q: A market research firm's dashboard team consistently hits its velocity targets. Clients rarely use the new dashboard features. What should the project manager do?
options: Increase the team's delivery pace to add more features
Raise the velocity target to deliver more features per sprint
Shift measures from team output to client usage and outcomes
Add tooltips and tutorials to the existing dashboard features
explain: Velocity measures output, not value. Measuring usage and outcomes redirects effort toward what clients actually need.

q: An AI startup's product teams make architecture decisions independently. Recently, two teams chose incompatible data platforms. What should the project manager do next?
options: Let the teams migrate later to whichever platform proves to be better
Route every team decision to a central architecture board
Require all decisions to pass through a central approval board
Establish lightweight decision rules for cross-team architecture
explain: Agile governance should be just enough. Lightweight rules prevent conflicts without heavy central control.

q: A content moderation tool's roadmap was set a year ago. The team now delivers every two weeks, and each release changes what the next most valuable work is. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Rebuild the roadmap from scratch at the end of every quarter instead
Hold to the annual roadmap and log new ideas for next year
Update the roadmap regularly based on what each release reveals
Keep the original roadmap and park new ideas for later
explain: Each release produces learning, so the plan must be maintained continuously. A frozen roadmap ignores value; quarterly rebuilds are too slow and wasteful.

q: A fitness chain restructures and moves the project's sponsor to a new role. The new sponsor has not yet been briefed. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Review the restructuring's effect before contacting the new sponsor
Brief the new sponsor and reconfirm objectives and support
Send the new sponsor the latest status report
Analyze how the restructuring changes the project's priorities
explain: The key impact is clear: a new sponsor. Engaging them to reconfirm objectives is the required action.

q: A car rental firm's telematics project must report finances to the CFO monthly and to the board quarterly. Formats were never agreed. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Agree on financial reporting formats and content with each audience
Report finances to both audiences within the regular project status report
Reuse the monthly CFO report as the quarterly board report
Send the CFO's monthly report to the board each quarter as well
explain: Financial reporting must be planned for each audience. Reusing one format ignores different needs.

q: A smart-lighting program involves city officials, vendors, and residents. Messages are consistent, but residents keep hearing about outages from social media first. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Issue more detailed outage notices on the city's official website
Ask the vendors to coordinate every outage message with the city officials first
Publish fuller outage information on the municipal web portal
Revise the communication strategy to reach residents through faster channels
explain: Content is consistent; timing and channel are the problem. The strategy must reach residents where and when they look.

q: A yacht builder's carpentry specialists are shared with another project. Both projects' schedules peak in the same month. What should the project manager do?
options: Coordinate with the other project to level the specialists' workload
Ask the other project to give your project priority on the specialists that month
Bring in temporary carpenters to cover the peak period
Hire additional carpenters for the peak month on short contracts
explain: Shared resources call for coordination across projects. Hiring specialists short-term is costly and slow; seeking priority just moves the conflict.

q: An audit-analytics team's junior product owner struggles to manage partner expectations. A senior product owner in another practice has offered to help. What should the project manager do next?
options: Enroll the junior product owner in stakeholder management training
Let the senior owner run the partner discussions
Have the senior product owner attend partner meetings instead
Set up a mentoring arrangement between the two product owners
explain: An offer of help is a mentoring opportunity to act on. Letting the senior person take over builds no capability, and generic training ignores the offer.

q: A ceramics plant's kiln control project passed every audit. A control chart now shows seven consecutive points above the mean, all within limits. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Widen the control limits to reflect the new process level
Take no action because the process stays within limits
Continue operating since all points remain within control limits
Investigate the cause since the pattern signals a process shift
explain: Seven consecutive points on one side of the mean indicate an assignable cause even within limits. It must be investigated.

q: A greenhouse expansion has a 30% chance of a heat event costing $200,000. The proposed response costs $40,000. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Accept the risk since its probability of occurring is below 50 percent
Implement the response since it costs less than the expected value
Analyze the heat event's probability once more before deciding
Review the probability estimate before committing to the response
explain: The expected monetary value is $60,000, more than the $40,000 response. The analysis is done; acting is justified.

q: A transit authority's ticketing app has reached the end of its funding. The product owner says the backlog still holds valuable stories. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Agree on closure criteria and transfer the backlog to the product owner
Continue sprints until the remaining backlog is complete
Keep delivering until all valuable stories are done
Archive the remaining backlog together with the closed project's records
explain: Funding has ended, so the project closes against agreed criteria. Remaining value moves with the product, not the project.

q: A watchmaker's assembly project collects lessons at closure. Team members say that by then they have forgotten key details. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Hold a longer lessons learned workshop at closure
Have the team record details for the final lessons meeting
Ask team members to keep notes for the closure session
Capture lessons throughout the project as they emerge
explain: Lessons should be captured continuously while details are fresh. Notes for a single session still delay their use.

q: A legal document-automation project closes next month. Lessons are logged diligently, but the firm's next project team says previous logs were never useful. What should the project manager do?
options: Make lessons searchable and walk the next team through the key ones
Send the final lessons log to the next team's project manager for reference
Expand each lesson entry with more background information
Log lessons in greater detail so the next team has more context
explain: Logs exist but are not used. Transfer needs accessibility and interaction; more detail in an unused log changes nothing.

q: A ski resort's lift project is funded in tranches tied to season revenue. A poor snow season is forecast. What should the project manager do next?
options: Keep spending as planned and adjust once funding is known
Proceed with the current spending plan until tranches are confirmed
Request a single lump-sum budget from the resort owners for the entire lift
Plan how funding shortfalls would affect the schedule and adjust early
explain: A foreseeable funding challenge should be anticipated. Waiting until money is short leaves fewer options.

q: An outpatient scheduling team agreed on a product vision with clinic managers in sprint zero. Six sprints later, a new chief nursing officer has joined and begun shaping priorities. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Revisit the product vision with the new officer and the clinic managers
Ask the product owner to absorb the officer's priorities into the backlog
Review the agreed vision with the officer to confirm she accepts it
Assess whether the officer's priorities fit the vision agreed in sprint zero
explain: A new key stakeholder can legitimately reshape the vision, so it must be revisited jointly. Reviewing or assessing against the old vision treats it as fixed, and absorbing priorities skips alignment.

q: A skincare launch team receives conflicting input: dermatologists want fewer ingredients, retail buyers want more claims. Both groups influence success. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Prioritize the dermatologists' input since they shape product credibility
Bring both groups' representatives together to reconcile priorities
Ask the product owner to split the line into two variants
Weight dermatologist feedback higher given its effect on credibility
explain: Both groups influence success, so favoring one leaves the other unaligned. Joint reconciliation optimizes alignment among needs and objectives.

q: A childcare provider's parent app stores children's photos. Developers suggest cloud storage abroad to cut costs. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Select the cheaper overseas option to meet budget targets
Check data residency obligations before choosing storage location
Choose the lower-cost storage to stay within the approved budget
Store the photos abroad and add strong encryption for their protection
explain: Children's data may carry strict residency rules. Consequences of noncompliance must be understood before deciding.

q: A veterinary chain's practice system project keeps documents in personal drives. Auditors could not locate the latest approved requirements. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Have document owners email current versions to auditors
Create an index listing which team member holds each one of the project files
Establish a controlled repository where approved artifacts are accessible
Ask each owner to send the latest documents to the auditors
explain: Artifacts must be accessible and controlled. Emailing files fixes one audit, not the practice.

q: A fertilizer plant upgrade team finds a vendor's delivered pump exceeds the specified capacity at no extra cost. Engineers want to use it. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept the pump because it adds capacity at no added cost
Evaluate the impact and process the deviation through change control
Return the pump to the vendor and request one that matches the specification
Install the higher-capacity pump since it costs nothing extra
explain: A free upgrade can still affect piping, power, or safety. Any deviation from the specified scope goes through change control.

q: An internet provider's teams produce a status report, a risk log, a decision log, and three dashboards. Few stakeholders read any of them. What should the project manager do next?
options: Send regular reminders encouraging stakeholders to read the reports
Combine all artifacts into one comprehensive weekly pack
Merge every artifact into a single weekly report
Keep the artifacts stakeholders actually use and retire the rest
explain: Artifacts should be tailored and their effectiveness assessed. Merging unused content does not make it useful.

q: A newspaper's digital subscription project faces resistance from senior editors who fear losing control over content. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Explain to editors that digital is the strategic direction
Communicate the strategic case for digital to editors
Run hands-on training for the senior editors on the new subscription platform
Involve senior editors in shaping how editorial control will work
