explain: Resistance rooted in loss of control is eased by involvement. Persuasion and training do not address the fear.

q: A tannery's improvement project produced a better wastewater procedure. The organization's procedure library still holds the old version. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Record the procedure in the project's lessons learned log
Update the organization's procedure library with the new version
Assess the new procedure with the team before wider use
Review the new procedure with the team before sharing it more widely
explain: The procedure is proven. Organizational process assets must be updated so future work uses it.

q: Two volunteer coordinators in a relief logistics team avoid each other after a disagreement. Delivery metrics are still on target, and neither has raised the issue. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Raise the topic in the next retrospective so the team can address it
Keep monitoring since delivery performance remains on target
Bring the issue to the team's next retrospective for discussion
Speak with each coordinator to understand the disagreement early
explain: Avoidance lets conflict grow even while metrics look fine. Addressing it early and privately is best; a retrospective exposes two people publicly.

q: A packaging line project's final deliverables are accepted. Team members have already been reassigned, and the financial records are incomplete. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Complete the financial closure and archive project records
Ask finance to finish the records once the project has formally closed
Review the acceptance records to confirm closure criteria
Assess acceptance documents to verify closure conditions
explain: Acceptance is done; financial closure is not. Financials must be concluded before closing.

q: A royalty-reporting feature team learns that independent labels receive release notes but never respond. The plan assumed silence means agreement. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Treat the labels as low-interest stakeholders in the register
Ask the labels to confirm receipt of each set of release notes
Find a channel and format that draws feedback from the labels
Send the release notes with a request to reply by a deadline
explain: Silence is not agreement. Communication has to be tailored to the labels' needs so real feedback flows.

q: Industrial customers of a grid modernization program were promised minimal outages. Monthly satisfaction scores are stable, but two key accounts stopped attending updates. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the current schedule of updates given the stable scores
Send the two accounts the update materials they missed
Contact the two accounts to understand why they disengaged
Continue the updates since overall satisfaction remains stable
explain: Averages can hide unhappy key customers. Disengagement is a signal to monitor and respond to directly.

q: A learning platform's teams each pull stories that serve the vision, but the sponsor says releases feel like three different products. Every story traces to an approved epic. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Make each epic's acceptance criteria stricter so teams interpret less
Tighten the acceptance criteria on each epic to reduce room for interpretation
Ask the sponsor to regroup the epics into one release theme
Hold a cross-team session to align on how the vision should feel to learners
explain: Traceability is intact, so scope control is not the issue. The teams lack a shared picture of the learner experience, which a joint vision session addresses.

q: A telehealth platform's internal clinicians want richer charts, while patients want fewer screens. The product owner has written both into the backlog. What should the project manager do next?
options: Build the clinician charts first since clinicians use it every day
Prioritize clinician needs because they spend more time in the tool
Deliver both requests in parallel using separate feature toggles for each
Validate a balanced design with clinicians and patients before building
explain: Internal and external customer expectations conflict. Validating a balanced outcome with both aligns them; favoring one group risks the other.

q: A bicycle maker's e-bike project shares a test rig with production. Test slots are preempted whenever production volume rises. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Buy a second test rig dedicated to the project
Agree with production on reserved test-rig slots for the project
Run tests during night shifts when production does not use the rig
Schedule testing outside production hours when the rig is idle
explain: Availability of the shared resource must be managed by agreement. Off-hours testing still depends on production volume.

q: A branch-closure program has a detailed engagement plan. Union representatives, classified to be kept informed, have started organizing petitions. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Prepare messaging that explains the closure rationale to those signing petitions
Change the engagement approach to work closely with union representatives
Analyze the petitions to identify the representatives' main objections
Review the petition content to see what the representatives oppose
explain: Petitions show the classification is outdated; the union now needs close management. Analyzing the petitions keeps the old distance.

q: A cloud migration epic is too large to finish in one iteration. The team keeps carrying it over, and stakeholders cannot see progress. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Split the epic into smaller stories that each deliver usable value
Extend the iteration length so the whole epic fits
Lengthen the sprint so the full epic can be completed
Assign additional developers to the epic so it finishes next iteration
explain: The epic needs to be broken down into deliverable slices. Longer sprints or more people treat the symptom and still hide progress.

q: A gas distribution project's sponsor verbally asks the project manager to add three valve stations, saying formal paperwork is unnecessary. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Evaluate the impact of the stations on budget and schedule
Submit the request through the change control process
Assess the stations' cost and schedule impact before proceeding
Add the stations as the sponsor asked
explain: Even the sponsor's request goes through change control. Impact analysis is part of that process, not a substitute.

q: An election commission's voter registration system is cancelled after a policy change. Half of the modules were delivered. What should the project manager do?
options: Pause the project in case the policy is reversed
Finish the outstanding modules to protect the spend so far
Document the delivered work and lessons, then formally close
Complete the remaining modules so the investment made is not lost
explain: A cancelled project still needs formal closure. Finishing it to save sunk costs ignores the decision.

q: During scope definition for a bottling line, the requirements traceability matrix shows several requirements with no linked business objective. What should the project manager do next?
options: Confirm with stakeholders whether those requirements belong in scope
Review the business case for objectives these requirements might serve
Link each requirement to the closest available objective
Analyze the objectives list to see where the requirements could link
explain: Only stakeholders can decide whether unlinked requirements belong. Searching for objectives to attach them to risks forcing traceability that does not exist.

q: An actuarial consultancy announces a merger midway through a modeling tool project. The merged firm may use a different platform. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Pause all work until the merger is complete
Continue as planned until the merged firm decides on platforms
Proceed with the current plan pending platform decisions
Evaluate the merger's impact on the project with the sponsor
explain: Organizational change can invalidate the project's direction. Its impact must be evaluated and actions determined.

q: An elevator modernization program has fixed hardware lead times but uncertain software requirements from building owners. The team must recommend a delivery approach. Which approach should the project manager recommend?
options: Plan hardware predictively and develop the software iteratively
Plan all work predictively and hold a buffer for software changes
Use a predictive approach with added contingency for software
Develop both hardware and software in short iterative releases
explain: Stable, long-lead hardware suits predictive planning, while uncertain software suits iteration. A hybrid approach fits the mixed profile better than either pure option.

q: A micromobility startup's backlog was set before the city announced new scooter parking rules. The rules take effect in two months. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Ask the city for an exemption during the pilot period
Add the parking rules to the backlog for a future product release
Log a story for the rules to address in later sprints
Reprioritize the backlog to address the new parking rules
explain: External changes must be reflected in backlog priority. Deferring them ignores the two-month deadline.

q: A fisheries monitoring project had identified a risk of permit delays. The permit authority has now formally announced a two-month backlog. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Add a new risk for possible further permit delays
Reassess the permit risk with a higher likelihood score
Treat it as an issue and implement the planned response
Review the permit risk and raise its probability rating accordingly
explain: The risk has occurred and is now an issue. Raising its probability treats a certainty as a possibility.

q: A trading-platform upgrade reports green status every month. A review shows the status reflects activity completion, not deliverable acceptance. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Redefine progress metrics so they reflect accepted deliverables
Report percent complete by activity in greater detail
Add activity-level detail to the monthly status report
Make the thresholds for each status color stricter going forward
explain: Metrics based on activity hide whether real value is accepted. Metrics must measure meaningful progress.

q: A roastery's new production line plan estimates effort using a sister plant's figures. The sister plant runs a different roasting technology. What should the project manager do?
options: Add a buffer on top of the sister plant's effort figures
Re-estimate with experts who know the new roasting technology
Apply a contingency percentage to the sister plant's estimates
Use the sister figures and refine them after the first month
explain: Analogous data from a different technology is not comparable. Padding a flawed basis keeps it flawed; expert judgment on the right technology fixes it.

q: A water main replacement affects a hospital, schools, and businesses. The register lists them all, but engagement levels were assessed before the pipe routing changed. What should the project manager do next?
options: Notify the registered stakeholders about the routing update
Add the routing change to the communications plan's next cycle
Inform the listed stakeholders of the new routing through usual channels
Reassess the stakeholders' engagement levels for the new routing
explain: The routing change alters who is affected and how much. Stakeholders must be analyzed again before engagement continues.

q: A robotics team's capacity dropped because two members were partly assigned to support work. The product owner still expects the planned sprint scope. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Remove the support work from the two members' assignments
Keep the planned scope and ask the team to work more efficiently
Plan the sprint based on the team's actual available capacity
Hold the sprint scope and look for efficiency gains instead
explain: Commitments must reflect real capacity. Keeping the scope sets the team up to fail, and reassigning support work may not be the team's decision.

q: An editorial platform's stakeholders each approved scope in separate meetings. A consolidated review now shows two departments believe different modules are included. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Include both modules in scope so each department's expectations are met
Hold a joint review so all departments agree on one scope baseline
Base the scope on the main funding department's approval
Use the scope approved by the department with the largest budget
explain: Separate approvals produced different understandings. Stakeholder agreement on one scope requires a joint review.

q: A bakery chain's oven replacement has used 70% of its contingency reserve at 40% completion. The remaining risks are rated high. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Use the management reserve to replenish contingency as needed
Draw on the management reserve to restore the contingency balance
Lower the remaining risk ratings so they match the reserve amount that is left
Reassess reserve adequacy against remaining risks and inform governance
explain: Reserves are being consumed faster than progress. Governance must be informed; management reserve is not the project manager's to use alone.

q: Stakeholders of a winery's export portal keep asking about their submitted change requests. Decisions are made, but requesters never hear back. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Speed up decisions so requesters see outcomes sooner
Process change requests faster so results become visible
Publish the change control procedure on the project site for stakeholders
Communicate each request's status and decision to its requester
explain: Decisions exist but are not communicated. The status of proposed changes must be shared.

q: A payroll provider is outsourcing part of a product build to a vendor. Requirements are expected to evolve sprint by sprint. How should the agreement be structured?
options: With a full specification up front to lock a fixed price
Around incremental deliveries that allow scope to flex
With payment on completion of the entire product
With scope fixed in detail before signing to secure price
explain: Evolving requirements suit an agile contract built on incremental delivery. Fixing scope early guarantees costly change orders.

q: A chemical plant expansion must now report carbon intensity to investors. The project management plan was baselined before this obligation existed. What should the project manager do?
options: Incorporate carbon reporting into the plan through change control
Add carbon metrics to the monthly status reports from next cycle
Include carbon intensity figures in the next set of status reports
Assign the carbon reporting duty to the sustainability department
explain: A new critical information requirement changes the baselined plan, so it must enter through change control. Adding it to reports alone leaves the plan inconsistent.

q: A pharmacy chain's prescription system has quality reviews at the end of each phase. Pilots show defects accumulate between reviews. What should the project manager do next?
options: Make each end-of-phase review more detailed and thorough
Extend the pilot to find defects before the reviews
Strengthen the end-of-phase reviews with deeper checks
Introduce ongoing quality reviews throughout each phase
explain: Defects build up between reviews, so reviews must be ongoing. Deeper end-of-phase reviews still find them late.

q: A serialization project at a drug plant is technically on track, yet operators keep calling it the compliance tax. Adoption after go-live depends on these same operators. What should the project manager focus on?
options: Reinforce the regulatory deadline that makes serialization mandatory
Remind operators that regulators require serialization by a set date
Add operator sign-off steps to the deployment checklist ahead of the go-live date
Connect the project's purpose to outcomes the operators value in their work
explain: Operators see no value for themselves, and adoption depends on them. Promoting the vision in terms they care about builds commitment; repeating the mandate breeds compliance at best.

q: A spice trading company's ERP team keeps waiting weeks for decisions. The charter does not name who approves scope trade-offs. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Clarify decision rights for trade-offs in the governance structure
Let the project manager decide trade-offs to save waiting time
Assign scope trade-off decisions to the project manager
Hold weekly meetings to collect and review all the pending decisions
explain: Undefined decision rights cause delay. Governance must define them, not shift them by assumption.

q: A terminal expansion depends on goodwill from nearby residents. Community leaders say they trust the project's contractor far more than its owner organization. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Involve the contractor's representatives in community engagement sessions
Publish the owner's commitments to residents on the project website
Review the owner's past interactions to learn why trust is lower
Assess why residents trust the owner organization less than the contractor
explain: The useful fact is already known: the contractor holds trust. Building on that relationship influences residents; investigating the reasons delays it.

q: A pet food subscription team has a working prototype. Marketing wants to wait for full features; the product owner wants early customer validation. What should the project manager support?
options: Delay release until all planned features are finished
Wait for the complete feature set to make a stronger launch
Demonstrate the working prototype to marketing for internal approval first
Release a minimum viable version to a customer segment for validation
explain: Early real-customer validation is the delivery option that best demonstrates value and reduces risk.

q: While planning a dam refurbishment, the operations director and the environmental officer both endorse the project, yet each describes success in terms the other does not recognize. What should the project manager do next?
options: Analyze how each leader's view of success would shape the project scope
Review each leader's success criteria against the approved business case
Bring both leaders together to agree on a single statement of project success
Record both leaders' definitions in the charter as complementary project objectives
explain: The differences are already known; what is missing is a shared vision among key stakeholders. Further review or analysis delays agreement, and recording both views keeps the split alive.

q: A podcast network's distributed team misses decisions made in ad hoc calls. Notes exist but are scattered across personal folders. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Ask each attendee to email call notes to the whole team
Limit decisions to scheduled meetings that everyone can attend
Have participants circulate their call notes to everyone after each meeting
Agree on a shared place where decisions are recorded and visible
explain: Decisions are recorded but scattered. One shared, visible record promotes transparency; more email multiplies the scattering.

q: A tire plant's equipment supplier is two weeks late. Liquidated damages apply, but the supplier is the only qualified source. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Assess the delay penalties due under the contract's terms
Begin qualifying an alternative supplier to be used for future orders
Review the contract to calculate the damages owed for the delay
Work with the supplier on recovery while preserving contract rights
explain: With a sole source, the relationship matters most. Calculating damages now does not recover the schedule; a joint recovery plan does, without waiving rights.

q: A frozen-meal plant upgrade must meet new food safety rules. The team has defined product specifications but not how compliance will be verified. What should the project manager do?
options: Review the specifications to confirm they reflect the new rules
Hire an external auditor to verify compliance once the upgrade is complete
Plan the verification methods needed to show regulatory compliance
Analyze the specifications against the rules for any gaps
explain: Specifications are already defined; the gap is how compliance will be demonstrated. Quality planning must define verification methods.

q: A vessel dry-docking schedule shows five days of negative variance. The planner proposes overlapping hull painting with the engine overhaul, which share no resources. What should the project manager do next?
options: Add shifts to the painting crew to recover the five days
Evaluate the rework risk of overlapping them, then fast-track if acceptable
Rebaseline the dry-docking schedule to reflect the five-day negative variance
Increase painting crew hours to make up the delay
explain: With no shared resources, fast-tracking is feasible but adds rework risk to check. Rebaselining hides the variance, and painting may not be critical.

q: A sports equipment brand's app project is ending. The team held retrospectives every sprint, and the sponsor asks whether a final lessons session is needed. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Hold a final session to capture project-wide lessons for the organization
Share the latest retrospective's findings with the sponsor as the final lessons
Use the existing retrospective outputs as the project lessons
Compile the sprint retrospective notes as the final lessons
explain: Sprint retrospectives focus on team process. A final session captures project-level lessons for the organization.

q: A retailer approved furniture prototypes, but its stores now report that assembled units differ from the showroom samples. Production follows the approved drawings. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Confirm to the retailer that the units conform to the approved drawings
Modify production so finished units match the showroom samples
Meet the retailer to reconcile how the samples and drawings diverged
Change the production process to reproduce the samples exactly
explain: Units follow the drawings, yet the retailer expected the samples. The expectation gap must be reconciled with the customer before changing production or defending the drawings.

q: An interior design firm's office fit-out is complete, and the client has signed acceptance. One subcontract still has an open payment dispute. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Examine the client's sign-off to verify closure can proceed
Resolve and close the open subcontract before closing the project
Review the client acceptance to confirm the project may close
Transfer the open payment dispute to the firm's finance department
explain: Client acceptance is confirmed; procurement closure is not. All contracts must be closed before the project is.

q: On a blast furnace relining, a crew lead reports that two members keep waiting for instructions because they assumed the vendor's supervisor was directing them. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Examine how daily instructions currently reach the two crew members
Hold a short daily briefing so that the whole crew hears the day's work plan
Review the crew's daily assignments with the vendor's supervisor
Clarify reporting lines and roles for the crew and the vendor supervisor
explain: The cause is already known: unclear roles. Reviewing assignments or examining the flow restates the problem; clarifying reporting lines resolves it.

q: A drone maker's procurement plan requires two qualified suppliers for critical components. The team has found one supplier that meets every specification. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Award the contract to the supplier meeting every specification
Evaluate whether the single supplier's capacity covers the full volume
Assess the supplier's capacity against volumes
Continue qualifying a second supplier as the plan requires
explain: The procurement plan sets a dual-source rule. Capacity checks on one supplier do not satisfy it.

q: Midway through a hangar digitization project, two shift leads describe the end goal differently in a retrospective, though both quote the charter word for word. What should the project manager do first?
options: Realign both teams' work to the sponsor's original success criteria
Reissue the charter with a clarified statement of the intended outcome
Explore with both leads how each one interprets the intended outcome
Rewrite the outcome section of the charter so it cannot be misread
explain: Both leads quote the same charter text, so the wording is not the gap; their interpretation is. Breaking the situation down to find the root cause of the misunderstanding comes before rewriting documents or realigning work.

q: A tunnel project is behind schedule. The team proposes adding crews to tasks with significant float to recover time. What should the project manager do?
options: Examine the float on each task before assigning extra crews
Focus recovery on critical path activities, not those with float
Review the float values to confirm which tasks have the most
Fast-track the activities that have float so the project saves time
explain: Only critical path activities drive the finish date. Float is already known; adding resources there wastes money.

q: An online store's team must choose between two features of similar effort. Analytics show one affects checkout conversion; the other was requested by the most senior executive. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Deliver the senior executive's feature first due to its backing
Prioritize the feature with measurable impact on checkout conversion
Build both features at reduced scope so they fit into the same release
Prioritize the executive's request given its sponsor-level support
explain: Value, not seniority, drives prioritization. The conversion data shows which feature delivers more value.

q: A battery-pack line team has become highly skilled and now challenges design choices with solid evidence. The project manager still assigns their daily tasks individually. What should the project manager change?
options: Let the team decide how to distribute daily work within agreed goals
Delegate daily task assignment to the most experienced members
Move task assignment to a weekly cadence with clearer priorities for all
Give the strongest members authority to assign tasks to the others
explain: A mature, evidence-driven team is ready for empowerment. Handing control to a few senior members simply creates a new hierarchy.

q: A clinic network's new project lacks defined success metrics. The sponsor says success will be obvious when it happens. What should the project manager do next?
options: Agree on measurable success metrics with the sponsor at the outset
Use on-time and on-budget delivery as the success measures
Measure success by schedule and cost performance
Define the success metrics after the first deliverable has been reviewed
explain: Success must be defined early and measurably. Time and cost alone do not show value.

q: A lab automation project needs a validation engineer for three months. The resource management plan says specialized roles are sourced through the PMO pool. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Recruit a contract validation engineer directly for three months
Request a validation engineer through the PMO's resource pool
Evaluate team skills to find who could validate
Assess whether a current member could be trained in validation
explain: The resource management plan already defines the sourcing route. Evaluating internal options or recruiting directly bypasses the plan.

q: An irrigation automation project is ending phase one. Phase two will use a new contractor team, and the phase one crew is being released next week. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Capture the critical knowledge now, before the crew is released
Assess the documentation for information phase two will need
Review the phase one documents for gaps the new contractor may face
Invite the phase two contractor to the phase one closing meeting
explain: The crew leaves next week, so the window is closing. Identifying and gathering critical knowledge from people comes first; documents can be reviewed later.

q: A game studio's three squads have drifted apart on the player experience they are building. The product vision board was last touched before the publisher's mid-cycle feedback arrived. What is the most appropriate action for the project manager?
options: Work with the product owner to refresh the vision using the publisher's input
Arrange a joint demo so the squads can see where their builds diverge
Have each squad translate the current vision board into its sprint goals
Ask each squad to restate the current vision board within its own sprint goals
explain: The board predates the publisher's feedback, so the vision is stale. Keeping the vision current fixes the source of drift; restating an outdated board or demoing differences does not.

q: An auto repair chain's app teams each run good retrospectives, but the same deployment problems appear across every team. Which action should the project manager take?
options: Assign the deployment problem to the most experienced team
Ask every team to discuss deployment in its retrospective
Have each team add the deployment issue to its own next retrospective
Hold a cross-team retrospective on the shared deployment problem
explain: A shared, system-level problem needs a cross-team improvement effort. Separate retrospectives lack the full picture.

q: A driving school's booking app team discusses risks informally. Two foreseeable problems recently surprised the product owner. What is the best way for the project manager to handle this?
options: Ask the team to report risks to the project manager privately
Schedule a dedicated risk review once a month
Make risks visible by adding risk items to the backlog
Hold a separate monthly risk meeting with the product owner
explain: Agile teams manage risk transparently through the backlog. A monthly meeting is too slow and separate from the work.

q: A lottery operator's app team is asked for a release date for a 400-point backlog. Velocity over the last five sprints ranged from 35 to 45. What should the project manager provide?
options: A committed date based on the average velocity of 40 points
A release window forecast from the observed velocity range
A single date calculated from the team's mean velocity
An optimistic date based on the highest velocity observed
explain: Velocity varies, so the forecast should be a range. A single date hides uncertainty.

q: A security firm's scheduling team was blocked by missing client data. The project manager arranged access, but the team still reports slow progress. What should the project manager do?
options: Review the access arrangement to confirm it was set up correctly
Add temporary capacity so the team can make up for the time it lost
Examine the access setup to verify it was completed properly
Check with the team whether the blocker is resolved or has shifted
explain: Impediments need continual reassessment from the team's view. Checking the setup alone misses what the team still faces.

q: A dental chain's booking app team is asked mid-sprint to add insurance verification. The product owner agrees it is valuable. What should the project manager do next?
options: Extend the current sprint so that insurance verification can fit in
Swap it into the current sprint for a lower-value story
Add it to the product backlog for the product owner to prioritize
Replace a lower-priority sprint item with the new feature
explain: Value does not justify disrupting the sprint commitment. New work goes to the backlog for prioritization in a coming sprint.

q: A property firm's building retrofit schedule was approved. The team now finds one activity duration was entered in days instead of weeks. How should the project manager proceed?
options: Correct the baseline through the change control process
Leave the baseline and track variance
Review the schedule for other entries with the same unit error
Assess all durations to confirm no further unit errors exist
explain: Any change to an approved baseline, even a correction, goes through change control. Checking other entries is sensible later but does not fix this one.

q: An HVAC retrofit in a hospital wing requires infection-control measures during work. The contractor's plan omits them. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Assess the contractor's work methods for infection exposure
Schedule the retrofit work for the hospital wing's lowest-occupancy hours
Review the contractor's methods to gauge the infection risk
Require the contractor's plan to include infection-control measures
explain: The requirement is known and the gap is clear. Compliance must be built into the plan.

q: A commercial tower owner needs a fit-out contractor, but the tenant's layout is still evolving. The owner wants to cap financial exposure. Which contract type is most appropriate?
options: A firm fixed-price contract based on the current layout
A time and materials contract with a not-to-exceed value
A cost-plus-fixed-fee contract covering all of the fit-out work
A lump-sum contract priced on the draft layout
explain: Evolving scope rules out fixed price, and open-ended cost-plus offers no cap. Time and materials with a ceiling fits both needs.
